hinweis: Reaction and convergence times of mentions markets after the content drop; exclusions listed separately. Medians are published per resolved outcome because YES and NO cases measure different mechanisms: a YES market reacts to an utterance that happened, a NO market decays as the remaining window empties. Method, data basis and caveats are in `quelle`.

quelle.methode: t0 is the start of the transmission (the content drop); price series of the YES token at fidelity=1 (minute grid). Baseline = median price of the 60 minutes before t0. First reaction = first minute at or after t0 whose price stands more than 1 point (0.01) away from that baseline, in either direction — it is a price move, not proof that anything was said. Convergence = first time the price durably stays past 0.9 (resolved YES) or below 0.1 (resolved NO) until the series ends. Tradeable window = hours after t0 in which the price stayed strictly between 0.1 and 0.9, measured on the price series independently of the reaction threshold — it can start before the first reaction (jre_vance_2221: window 0.08 h against a reaction-to-convergence span of 0.03 h) and is not convergence minus reaction.
quelle.datengrundlage: 12 curated status-ok cases plus one documented exclusion from the thesis file data/results/mentions_latency.csv. Each case carries its drop timestamp (t0), Polymarket condition id, and the exact second gaps (sekunden_*): reaction/convergence epoch of the minute-grid price point minus the curated drop epoch — the minute values are these gaps rounded to 0.1 min, which is why e.g. 11.5 s median (exact) and 0.15 min (rounded pooled median, published as 0.2 in kategorie_karte.json) coexist. The minute-grid price series live in the thesis repository's raw cache and are not republished here.
einschraenkungen: Convergence contains the time until the resolution-relevant statement inside the broadcast: a word said in minute 90 makes convergence at least 90 minutes without the market being slow. Every convergence figure is an upper bound on reaction speed, not a reaction time.

YES and NO cases measure different mechanisms. YES reacts to an utterance that happened (median first reaction 0.1 min). A NO market has no triggering event: its first 1-point move (median 4.0 min) is drift, and it can only converge once the broadcast is (almost) over. The pooled medians mix both; compare per outcome.

A first reaction counts any move of more than 1 point off the pre-drop baseline, in either direction: in 6 of the 12 cases the first move went AWAY from the outcome that later resolved (flagged per case as erste_reaktion_zum_outcome=false). Do not read a many-minute first reaction as 'the condition was met and the market was slow' — every first reaction above one minute in this sample belongs to a NO market, where the resolving utterance never happened at all.

The three slowest first reactions (7.2, 10.3 and 86.7 min) all sit on cases whose drop timestamp is only hour-precise (scheduled start of the broadcast), so part of those minutes can be t0 imprecision rather than market behaviour.

Second-level figures are exact timestamp arithmetic, not tick-level latency: the price series has one point per minute (fidelity=1), so a reaction of '7 s' means the first minute-grid point after t0 already stood more than 1 point off baseline — the true first trade can lie anywhere inside that minute. Several drop timestamps are additionally only hour-precise.
The 1-point threshold has no placebo baseline: how often such a move occurs in a quiet window of comparable books was not counter-tested, so in thin books a 'first reaction' can be noise.
n = 12 hand-picked events, not a random sample; selection favours broadcasts with a clean, documentable drop timestamp.

Frozen snapshot of 2026-08-07 — the generator lives in the thesis repository, not here, and mentions events keep happening weekly; nothing after that date is measured. All 12 rows, the medians and the resolved outcomes were re-verified against the thesis raw price cache on 2026-08-27; each resolved outcome matches the final price of its own market series.
